title: Ectoderm Embryology and Skin Development
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows the ectoderm as it splits into surface ectoderm, neuroectoderm, and neural crest, then traces how the skin, its appendages, and its pigment cells form before birth. Board questions usually name a structure and ask for its germ layer, or describe a newborn skin finding or pigment disorder and ask where development went wrong. The unifying idea is that melanocytes are migrants: they start at the neural tube and must travel, survive, and then make melanin. Knowing which of those steps failed explains a blue sacral patch, a white forelock, and generalized albinism.
prerequisites: The three germ layers and gastrulation
Somite organization into sclerotome and dermomyotome
Epidermal layers, melanocytes, and adnexa of adult skin (IN-1)

connections.how: Neurulation creates the neural tube and releases the neural crest, so neural tube and crest defects share their origin in the same event.
The adult epidermis, follicle, and glands described there are built by the developmental steps in this chapter.
Vitiligo, albinism, and nevi are classified by whether melanocytes are missing, present but inactive, or proliferating.
The anterior and posterior pituitary, adrenal medulla, and thyroid C cells come from three different ectodermal lineages.
Hirschsprung disease is a failure of neural crest migration to the distal bowel, the enteric counterpart of piebaldism.

terms.def: Ectoderm that remains outside the neural plate and forms the epidermis, its appendages, and several sensory and oral epithelia.
Ectoderm of the neural plate that folds into the neural tube and forms the central nervous system, retina, and posterior pituitary.
Cells from the border of the neural plate that undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and migrate to form many peripheral tissues.
The loss of cell junctions and polarity that lets an epithelial cell become a motile mesenchymal cell.
The dorsal part of a somite, which gives rise to the dermis of the back (dermatome) and to skeletal muscle (myotome).
A temporary superficial layer of flattened fetal epidermal cells that covers the developing epidermis and is later shed.
A neural crest-derived precursor of the melanocyte that is still migrating and does not yet make melanin.
A condensation of mesenchyme at the base of the hair bud that signals to the epithelium to form and grow the hair.
Fine, unpigmented first fetal hair, appearing around the fifth month and mostly shed before or around birth.
A whitish fetal skin coating of sebum, shed periderm and epidermal cells, and water that protects the skin in amniotic fluid.
Scattering of shorter blue wavelengths by tissue, which makes melanin deep in the dermis appear blue-gray instead of brown.
The receptor tyrosine kinase for stem cell factor, required for melanoblast survival, proliferation, and migration.

sections.title: Surface ectoderm, neuroectoderm, and neural crest

blocks.text: After gastrulation, the ectoderm is a single sheet on the dorsal surface of the embryo. Around day 18 to 19, the notochord and prechordal mesoderm secrete noggin, chordin, and follistatin, which block bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) in the overlying ectoderm. Ectoderm with low BMP signaling thickens into the neural plate (neuroectoderm); ectoderm that keeps high BMP signaling becomes surface ectoderm. The neural plate folds, and its edges fuse in the midline starting in the future cervical region, forming the neural tube.

Cells at the border between the plate and surface ectoderm receive intermediate BMP signals together with Wnt and fibroblast growth factor signals. They express transcription factors such as SNAI2 (Slug), SOX10, and PAX3, lose their epithelial junctions, and migrate away as neural crest. Cranial crest begins migrating before the folds fuse; trunk crest leaves as the tube closes. Because all three lineages arise from one sheet in one event, a single developmental error can affect the brain, the skin, and crest derivatives together.

blocks.caption: Microglia are the exception in the CNS: they come from yolk sac macrophage precursors (mesoderm), not neuroectoderm.

blocks.text: Several pairs of adjacent structures have different origins. The anterior pituitary grows up from the roof of the primitive mouth (Rathke pouch, surface ectoderm), while the posterior pituitary grows down from the diencephalon (neuroectoderm); remnants of Rathke pouch give rise to craniopharyngioma. In the eye, the lens and corneal epithelium are surface ectoderm, but the retina and its pigment epithelium are outgrowths of the brain. In the tooth, enamel is surface ectoderm while dentin is made by crest-derived odontoblasts.

Surface ectoderm also forms placodes, local thickenings that give rise to the lens, the otic vesicle (inner ear membranous labyrinth), the olfactory epithelium, and some sensory neurons of cranial nerve ganglia V, VII, IX, and X, which share these ganglia with neural crest. Mammary glands bud from paired mammary ridges (milk lines) of surface ectoderm running from axilla to groin; extra nipples (polythelia) appear along this line. Skin appendages arise from shared placode signaling, which is why X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (EDA gene) causes sparse hair, absent sweat glands with heat intolerance, and missing or conical teeth together.

blocks.predict: A child has a lens defect and a pituitary tumor arising from the sella that contains calcifications. Which shared germ layer links the lens and this tumor?
blocks.explain: Surface ectoderm. The lens forms from the lens placode, and craniopharyngioma arises from remnants of Rathke pouch, an upgrowth of oral surface ectoderm. The posterior pituitary and retina, by contrast, are neuroectoderm.

sections.title: Neural crest derivatives and the regional origin of the dermis

blocks.text: Neural crest cells are multipotent, and their fate depends largely on the route they take and the signals they meet. In the trunk, crest cells follow two main routes. The ventral pathway runs through the rostral half of each sclerotome; cells on it become dorsal root ganglia, sympathetic chain ganglia, Schwann cells, and chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. The dorsolateral pathway runs between the dermomyotome and the surface ectoderm; cells on it become melanoblasts. Vagal and sacral crest colonize the gut wall as enteric ganglia.

blocks.caption: The route determines the fate: ventral cells form neurons, glia, and chromaffin cells, and dorsolateral cells form pigment cells.

blocks.text: Why facial dermis is neural crest and back dermis is somitic

The epidermis is surface ectoderm everywhere, but the dermis forms from whatever mesenchyme lies beneath it, and that mesenchyme differs by region. Somites begin in the occipital region, so there are no somites under the face. Instead, cranial neural crest streams into the frontonasal process and pharyngeal arches and forms most of the facial mesenchyme, which becomes facial bone, cartilage, connective tissue, and dermis. Over the back, each somite's dermomyotome releases dermatome cells that spread beneath the overlying ectoderm and form the dorsal dermis. In the limbs and ventral body wall, the dermis comes from the somatic layer of lateral plate mesoderm.

blocks.title: Origin of the two skin layers by region
blocks.caption: In every region, the epidermis and dermis of the same patch of skin can come from different germ layers.

blocks.text: Dermal mesenchyme signals to the overlying epidermis and helps decide what kind of appendages form, so the dermis shapes regional skin character. Do not confuse the embryonic dermatome (the part of a somite that forms dorsal dermis) with the clinical dermatome (the skin area supplied by one spinal nerve): limb skin has a segmental nerve supply even though its dermis is lateral plate mesoderm.

blocks.title: Working out the origin of one patch of skin
blocks.text: Take a biopsy from the cheek and one from the skin over the lower thoracic spine. Both epidermal layers are surface ectoderm, and the melanocytes in both are neural crest. The difference lies in the dermis. The cheek lies over the first pharyngeal arch, which has no somites beneath it and is filled with cranial crest mesenchyme, so its dermis is neural crest. The back lies directly over the somites, so its dermis comes from somite dermatomes, which is paraxial mesoderm. A forearm biopsy would differ again, since limb buds are built from lateral plate mesoderm.

Fetal skin turns a single sheet of surface ectoderm into a stratified, keratinized barrier in a fixed order. During the second month, that single layer divides into a deep basal (germinative) layer and a superficial periderm of flattened cells, which seals the embryo while the layers beneath it mature. Proliferation of the basal layer then adds an intermediate layer, and by about the end of the fourth month the epidermis has its definitive arrangement of basal, spinous, granular, and cornified layers. As keratinization proceeds, periderm cells are shed into the amniotic fluid.

The barrier is not mature until late gestation. The stratum corneum becomes an effective barrier at about 32 to 34 weeks, so a very preterm infant has thin, permeable skin that loses water and heat quickly and absorbs substances applied to it more readily.

blocks.caption: Timings are approximate and vary slightly between embryology texts.

blocks.text: Melanoblasts from the neural crest migrate under the surface ectoderm, cross the dermis, and enter the epidermis during the first trimester, where they settle among basal cells and in developing hair bulbs. They begin producing melanin in fetal life, but skin color continues to darken after birth as melanin production increases.

Hair forms through reciprocal signaling between epithelium and mesenchyme. Basal cells thicken into a placode, which grows down into the dermis as a hair bud. Dermal mesenchyme condenses at the tip of the bud as the dermal papilla, and the bud end invaginates around it to form the bulb. The papilla then signals the surrounding matrix cells to divide and produce the hair shaft. Sebaceous glands bud from the side of the follicle wall, and the bulge forms below them, where the arrector pili muscle (from mesenchyme) attaches. The first hairs, lanugo, are fine and unpigmented; most are shed into the amniotic fluid late in gestation and are replaced by vellus and terminal hairs. Preterm infants are often still covered in lanugo.

blocks.title: Hair follicle formation
steps: Basal cells thicken into a hair placode

Bud end invaginates around the papilla to form the bulb

Sebaceous gland buds from the follicle wall
blocks.caption: The dermal papilla instructs the epithelium; without it, no hair shaft forms.

blocks.text: Fetal sebaceous glands are active in late gestation under androgen stimulation. Their sebum mixes with shed periderm and epidermal cells, water, and lanugo to form vernix caseosa, a whitish coat that protects the skin from maceration during months in amniotic fluid. Vernix also contains antimicrobial proteins and helps moisturize the skin after birth. A post-term infant often has little vernix left and shows dry, peeling skin, while a preterm infant may have vernix but an immature barrier beneath it.

sections.title: Dermal melanocytosis and other newborn skin lesions

blocks.text: Melanoblasts reach the epidermis by crossing the dermis, and almost all dermal melanocytes normally disappear or move on by birth. Some persist, most often over the lumbosacral region and buttocks. These arrested dermal melanocytes are spindle-shaped, lie deep in the reticular dermis, and keep making melanin. The result is dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spot): a flat, uniform, blue-gray patch present at birth. It is common in infants of Asian, African, Native American, and Hispanic descent and uncommon in those of European descent. Most patches fade during early childhood, though those outside the sacral area more often persist.

The color is explained by depth. Epidermal melanin absorbs most visible light and looks brown, while deep dermal melanin is reached mainly by longer wavelengths and the shorter blue wavelengths scatter back from the tissue above it (the Tyndall effect), so the patch looks blue-gray. The same principle colors blue nevi. Because a sacral or extensive patch can be mistaken for bruising in suspected child abuse, documenting it at birth matters. Unlike a bruise, it does not change color over days and is not tender.

blocks.caption: The lesion is benign; its color comes from the depth of the pigment, not from a different pigment.

blocks.text: Three other common newborn lesions are separated by the cell involved and by their course. A congenital melanocytic nevus is a proliferation of nevus cells present from fetal life, often reaching deep into the dermis and around adnexa, so it is brown and may grow coarse hair; large and giant lesions carry increased melanoma risk. An infantile hemangioma is a benign proliferation of GLUT1-positive endothelium, so it is absent or faint at birth, grows rapidly for months, then involutes over years. A port-wine stain is a capillary malformation of mature, dilated dermal capillaries and venules, usually from a somatic GNAQ mutation, so it is present at birth, grows only in proportion to the child, never regresses, and tends to darken and thicken in adulthood. Unilateral involvement of the ophthalmic (V1) distribution can accompany leptomeningeal and ocular vascular malformation (Sturge-Weber syndrome), with seizures and glaucoma. Nevus simplex, the far more common faint midline patch on glabella, eyelids, or nape, fades over the first years and carries no such risk.

blocks.predict: A newborn has a unilateral red patch covering one side of the forehead and the upper eyelid, fully formed at birth and grown only in proportion at 6 months. A second infant has no lesion at birth but a rapidly enlarging red nodule at 6 weeks. Which lesion will regress?
blocks.explain: The second. A lesion that appears after birth and grows faster than the child is an infantile hemangioma, a proliferating endothelial tumor that later involutes. The first is a port-wine stain, a capillary malformation that never regresses, and its V1 location raises concern for Sturge-Weber syndrome.

blocks.text: A white patch of skin can arise in three ways: melanocytes never arrived (piebaldism), they arrived but cannot make melanin (albinism), or they were destroyed after arriving (vitiligo).

Melanoblasts depend on the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase. Its ligand, stem cell factor, is produced along their migratory route, and KIT signaling keeps melanoblasts alive and drives their proliferation and migration. Piebaldism is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a loss-of-function KIT mutation. With reduced signaling, melanoblasts fail to reach the sites farthest from their dorsal origin or to survive there. Those sites lack melanocytes permanently, giving a white forelock and white patches on the central forehead, ventral trunk, and mid-arms and legs, usually sparing the back, hands, and feet. The patches are stable for life and often contain islands of normal or darker pigment. Biopsy shows absent or nearly absent melanocytes.

Oculocutaneous albinism is autosomal recessive and affects pigment synthesis, not migration. Melanocyte number and distribution are normal, but melanin output is reduced. In type 1, tyrosinase, the copper-dependent enzyme that converts tyrosine to DOPA and DOPA to dopaquinone, is absent or deficient. Other types involve proteins needed for melanosome function, such as the OCA2 (P) protein. Because every melanocyte is affected, hypopigmentation involves all skin, hair, and eyes.

blocks.title: Melanin synthesis and where albinism fails
steps: Tyrosine enters the melanosome
Tyrosinase converts tyrosine to DOPA
Tyrosinase converts DOPA to dopaquinone
Dopaquinone forms eumelanin or pheomelanin
Melanosomes transfer to keratinocytes
blocks.caption: Type 1 albinism blocks the first two steps; the melanocytes are present but produce little or no melanin.

blocks.text: The eye findings show where pigment matters for development. The retinal pigment epithelium is neuroectoderm, not neural crest, but it uses tyrosinase too, so albinism reduces its pigment. Melanin is needed for normal foveal development and for routing of optic nerve fibers, so albinism causes foveal hypoplasia, excessive crossing of fibers at the optic chiasm, nystagmus, reduced acuity, and photophobia with iris transillumination. Lacking melanin, the skin has little protection from ultraviolet light and develops sun damage and carcinomas, especially squamous cell carcinoma. In piebaldism the eyes are normal, because the retinal pigment epithelium does not depend on crest migration. When a crest disorder does affect the eye and ear, as in Waardenburg syndrome (PAX3, MITF, SOX10), iris heterochromia and deafness appear, since melanocytes of the iris stroma and cochlear stria vascularis are crest-derived.

blocks.caption: Count the melanocytes first, then ask whether the defect is present at birth and whether it is localized or generalized.

blocks.title: Two pale children
blocks.text: Child A has a white forelock and white patches on the abdomen and knees since birth, with normal eyes; a parent has the same forelock. Child B has white hair, very pale skin everywhere, and nystagmus; both parents are normally pigmented. In A, the patchy, stable pattern and dominant inheritance point to piebaldism, and a biopsy of a white patch would show no melanocytes, because melanoblasts never colonized those ventral and distal sites. In B, the generalized pattern, eye findings, and unaffected carrier parents point to recessive albinism. A biopsy would show melanocytes in normal numbers that make little melanin, and in type 1 the defect is tyrosinase.

integration.text: Embryology and genetics explain the patterns. The ectoderm splits into three lineages in one event, so the same signaling defect can involve skin, nervous system, and crest derivatives, as in ectodermal dysplasias and Waardenburg syndrome. Neural crest cells share migration machinery, which is why defects in genes such as SOX10 or EDNRB can produce pigment loss, deafness, and Hirschsprung disease together, and why piebaldism and Hirschsprung disease are both failures of crest colonization. Regional dermal origin (crest, somite, or lateral plate) explains why facial anomalies follow pharyngeal arch boundaries and why dorsal dermis is organized segmentally.

Biochemistry and pathology explain the pigment findings. Melanin synthesis begins at tyrosinase, so tyrosinase loss gives albinism, and in untreated phenylketonuria, low tyrosine and high phenylalanine reduce melanin and lighten hair and skin. Histology answers most pigment questions: absent melanocytes (piebaldism, vitiligo), normal melanocytes with little pigment (albinism), or melanocytes in the wrong place (dermal melanocytosis). The limits are clinical: a Mongolian spot cannot be told from a bruise by color alone, and only the course over weeks separates an early hemangioma from a capillary malformation.

summary: BMP inhibition from the notochord makes neural plate; high BMP leaves surface ectoderm; the border forms neural crest by epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.
Surface ectoderm forms epidermis, hair, nails, cutaneous and mammary glands, lens, corneal epithelium, anterior pituitary, and enamel.
Neuroectoderm forms CNS neurons and macroglia, retina and pigment epithelium, posterior pituitary, and pineal gland; microglia are mesodermal.
Neural crest forms melanocytes, Schwann cells, peripheral ganglia, adrenal medulla, odontoblasts, and facial mesenchyme including facial dermis.
Dermis comes from cranial crest in the face, somite dermatomes in the back, and lateral plate mesoderm in the limbs and ventral body wall.
Fetal epidermis passes from one layer to basal layer plus periderm to adult layers by about the fourth month; the barrier matures at about 32 to 34 weeks.
The dermal papilla induces hair formation; lanugo appears around the fifth month, and vernix is sebum plus shed cells that protects skin in amniotic fluid.
Dermal melanocytosis is arrested dermal melanocytes that look blue-gray by the Tyndall effect and usually fade; it must not be mistaken for bruising.
Infantile hemangioma (GLUT1 tumor) appears after birth, grows, and involutes; port-wine stain (GNAQ malformation) is present at birth and persists.
Piebaldism (dominant KIT) lacks melanocytes in stable patches with normal eyes; albinism (recessive, tyrosinase in type 1) has normal melanocytes that make little melanin.

Some texts describe the neural crest contribution to dermis as face and neck, others as face only; confirm the expected wording against current NABNE materials.
The neural crest origin of thyroid C cells is the classic teaching but has been questioned by lineage studies suggesting an endodermal origin; confirm which the exam expects.

Timing of first melanin production by fetal melanocytes varies by source and was not stated as a specific week.

Review-level sources often list pia and arachnoid as neural crest without qualification, while lineage studies limit the crest contribution to the forebrain leptomeninges and assign the rest to mesoderm; the restricted wording is used here.
